reasoning.Student A:
My goal is to maximize my utility, which is represented by the dollar values assigned to each school. However, I can only be matched to a school within my "obtainable" set. My priority rank at each school influences which schools are likely to be in my obtainable set.

I have high priority (rank 1) at schools w and y. I have lower priority (rank 2) at schools x and z. Given the general preference order of y > x > w > z, it's likely that many applicants will also prefer y. This means that even with high priority at y, it's not guaranteed I will be matched there.

School w is also desirable (value $70) and I have high priority there. Since most applicants favor y > x > w > z, it is likely that w will be less competitive than y. Thus, I have a good chance of being matched to w.

Schools x and z have lower values and lower priority for me. They are less desirable than w and y.

Therefore, I should rank the schools in decreasing order of value, but considering my high priority at w and y. I will rank y first, as it has the highest value and I have high priority. I will rank w second, as it also has high value and high priority. Then I will rank x, and lastly z.
reasoning.Student B:
My goal is to maximize my value by getting into the best school possible. My values are w = $74, x = $77, y = $63, z = $56. Clearly, I prefer x and w over y and z.

My priorities are: w: 2, x: 1, y: 2, z: 1. This means I have the highest priority at x and z.

Since x has the highest value ($77) and I have the highest priority there, it's my top choice.

Next, w has a higher value than y and z. While I have higher priority at z than w, the value difference between w and z ($74 vs $56) is significant enough that I'd rather rank w higher, even with a slightly lower chance of getting in.

Finally, I prefer y to z, so I rank y third and z last.

Therefore, my ranking is x > w > y > z.
reasoning.Student C: My values for w and x are the same ($70), and both are higher than y ($64) and z ($44). Therefore, I prefer w and x over y and z. Between w and x, my priority rank is the same (3). So I am indifferent between w and x. I will rank them arbitrarily. I prefer y over z because $64 > $44, so I will rank y higher than z. Therefore, my ranking is x > w > y > z.
